verses.context: The chapter opens where 29:31 left off: Rachel is loved but childless, and her envy breaks out as a demand on her husband. Jacob's angry answer is true, but it ends the conversation rather than turning it toward God, and it sets the tone for a chapter of rivalry.
verses.grammar: "She envied" is vattqanne, a Piel of qana, the verb for jealousy or zeal, the same root used of God's jealousy for his people. Rachel's words are two blunt clauses: havah-li vanim ("Give me children") and ve'im-ayin metah anokhi, literally ‘and if not, I am a dead woman’. Metah is a participle, ‘dying’, which gives the phrase a sense of present condition, not just a threat. The irony is heavy for the reader who knows 35:16-19: Rachel will die giving birth to her second son. Jacob's reply, hatachat Elohim anokhi ("Am I in the place of God"), is the exact question Joseph will ask his brothers in 50:19, where it expresses humility rather than anger. "Withheld" is mana, with the object peri-baten, ‘fruit of the womb’.

theology.note: Jacob states the right doctrine at the wrong moment: life in the womb is God's to give or withhold. The contrast with his father is pointed. When Rebekah was barren, Isaac prayed for her and the LORD answered (25:21); Jacob answers his wife's anguish with anger and a theological statement, and no prayer is recorded.

verses.context: Rachel turns to the recognized remedy for a barren wife and gives Jacob her servant Bilhah. The words deliberately echo Sarah's plan with Hagar in 16:2, a plan that ended in bitterness. Bilhah conceives at once.
verses.grammar: Rachel wants Bilhah to give birth al-birkai, ‘on my knees’. The phrase is widely understood as a gesture of adoption or acknowledgment: a child placed on the knees is claimed as one's own, as Joseph's great-grandchildren were ‘brought up on Joseph's knees’ (50:23). Ve'ibbaneh gam-anokhi mimmennah ("through her I too can build a family") is literally ‘I too will be built from her’. The verb banah, ‘build’, is a play on ben, ‘son’, and Sarah used the same verb with the same hope (16:2). Rachel calls Bilhah her amah in verse 3, and the narrator calls her shifchah in verse 4; the two words for a female servant are used interchangeably here.
verses.history: The arrangement is attested outside the Bible. The Laws of Hammurabi, from Babylon around 1750 BC, include provisions for a wife of a certain priestly class who gives her husband a slave woman to bear children, and a marriage contract from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia (fifteenth century BC) requires a childless wife to provide her husband with a slave woman. Such texts show the custom was widespread, not that Genesis borrowed from any one of them.

verses.context: Rachel names Bilhah's son Dan and explains the name as a verdict in her favor. She speaks as if she has won a case against her sister, and she credits God with hearing her.
verses.grammar: Dananni Elohim ("God has vindicated me") uses the verb din, ‘to judge’ or ‘to plead a case’, and the name Dan is its echo. Judging in Hebrew often means doing justice for someone, taking up their cause, so Rachel's claim is that God has ruled on her side. Vegam shama beqoli, "He has heard my plea", is literally ‘he has also listened to my voice’, which implies that Rachel had been praying. Jacob's blessing on Dan returns to the same root: "Dan shall provide justice for his people" (49:16).

theology.note: Rachel's words assume that she has prayed and that God has heard. The narrator reports her interpretation without endorsing her sense of victory over her sister; the verse shows a real prayer answered while the heart that prayed it is still tangled in rivalry.

verses.context: Bilhah bears a second son, and Rachel names him Naphtali with the most combative words in the chapter. Her boast of wrestling and winning looks ahead to the night at the Jabbok, where her husband will wrestle for a blessing.
verses.grammar: Naftule Elohim niftalti is literally ‘wrestlings of God I have wrestled’. Interpreters read Elohim here two ways. It may be a superlative, as Hebrew sometimes attaches God's name to express the greatest degree (compare ‘a mountain of God’ for a very high mountain), which is how the BSB takes it: "In my great struggles". Or it may mean struggles concerning God, a contest over God's favor as shown in children. The last verb, gam-yakholti, ‘and I have prevailed’, is the same verb the man at the Jabbok uses of Jacob: "you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed" (32:28). Rachel's claim of victory is premature; Jacob's will be won with a wound.

verses.context: Leah, who has stopped bearing, answers in kind and gives Jacob her servant Zilpah. The contest now involves four women, and the second servant bears Gad, a name about good luck.
verses.grammar: Leah's exclamation in verse 11 is a single word or two in Hebrew, and the name Gad (‘fortune, good luck’) is its point. Leah's reason is not answered prayer but good fortune, a striking change from the God-centered names of her first four sons. Verse 9 repeats the vocabulary of 29:35, amedah milledet, ‘she had stood still from bearing’, to show that this move follows directly from the pause at the end of chapter 29.
verses.text: The written Hebrew text (the Ketiv) has one word, begad, ‘with fortune’ or ‘in good fortune’; the Masoretes, the medieval scribes who added vowels and reading notes, marked it to be read as two words, ba gad, ‘fortune has come’. English versions follow one or the other: the KJV has ‘a troop cometh’, taking gad in a different sense, while most modern translations, the BSB among them, render it as an exclamation of good fortune.
verses.history: Gad was also the name of a Semitic god of fortune. Isaiah condemns those who "set a table for Fortune" (Isaiah 65:11), where the Hebrew word is gad, and place names such as Baal-gad (Joshua 11:17) and Migdal-gad (Joshua 15:37) probably preserve it. Leah's word need not invoke a deity; in her mouth it most naturally means luck.

verses.context: Zilpah bears a second son, Asher, and Leah names him for happiness. For the first time her naming speech looks outward to other women's opinion rather than to her husband or to God.
verses.grammar: Be'oshri ("How happy I am") is literally ‘in my happiness’, and ishsheruni banot is ‘daughters call me happy’. The verb is a Piel of ashar, the root of the word ashre, ‘blessed’ or ‘happy is’, that opens Psalm 1. It is a perfect in form but the BSB, like most translations, renders it with a present or future sense, ‘women call me happy’: Hebrew can use the perfect for an action the speaker regards as certain. Proverbs 31:28 uses the same verb for the children who "call her blessed", and Mary's words in Luke 1:48 carry the same idea in Greek.

verses.context: A boy's find in a wheat field becomes a bargaining chip. Reuben brings mandrakes to his mother, Rachel asks for some, and the sisters' exchange lays bare their grievances: Leah feels robbed of her husband, and Rachel controls who sleeps with him.
verses.grammar: Duda'im ("mandrakes") sounds like dodim, ‘love’ or ‘lovemaking’, which is part of why the plant was prized. Leah's retort begins hame'at, ‘is it a small thing’, a Hebrew idiom for ‘is it not enough’ (the same idiom Moses uses to Korah in Numbers 16:9). Her charge is qachtekh et-ishi, ‘your taking my husband’, an infinitive with a suffix that makes Rachel the subject of the taking. Rachel's reply opens with lakhen, ‘therefore’ or ‘very well then’, and continues with yishkav immakh hallaylah, ‘he will lie with you tonight’: she speaks of Jacob as a resource she can allot. The word tachat (‘in exchange for’) is the same word Jacob used in verse 2, ‘in the place of God’.
verses.history: The wheat harvest in the land of Israel and Syria fell in late spring, around May and June, when mandrake fruit is ripe. Reuben is a young boy here, since the sons were born within a few years of one another, and the scene is domestic and ordinary: a child brings his mother something he found in the field.

verses.context: Leah meets Jacob on his way in from the fields and tells him he has been hired for the night. The patriarch who once bought a birthright with a bowl of stew is now himself the thing bought, paid for with a handful of plants.
verses.grammar: Sakhor sekhartikha, "I have hired you", pairs an infinitive absolute with a finite form of the same verb, a common Hebrew way of adding emphasis: ‘I have indeed hired you’ or ‘I have paid for you fair and square’. The root sakhar (‘hire, wages’) will give the name Issachar in verse 18 and reappears in Laban's ‘name your wages’ in verse 28. Elay tavo, ‘to me you will come’, puts ‘to me’ first for emphasis. Jacob is given no words at all; the narrator simply says he lay with her.

verses.context: God, not the mandrakes, gives Leah a fifth son. Leah names him Issachar and interprets the birth as God's payment to her for giving Zilpah to Jacob, a reading the narrator records without adopting.
verses.grammar: Vayyishma Elohim el-Le'ah ("God listened to Leah") uses the same verb as the name Simeon (29:33) and implies that Leah had prayed. Her words natan Elohim sekhari ("God has rewarded me") use sakhar, ‘wages, hire’, the noun from the verb in verse 16: she was paid for her maid, and she paid for her husband. The name Issachar is heard as yesh sakhar, ‘there is a reward’, or ish sakhar, ‘man of hire’.
verses.text: The Hebrew consonants of the name Issachar are written with two s-sounds (Yissaskar), but the Masoretic reading tradition pronounces only one, Yissakhar, throughout the Bible. It is one of the few names that is always read differently from how it is written, and scholars have explained the spelling as preserving both explanations of the name.

theology.note: The narrator says God listened to Leah before anything is said about the mandrakes, which Rachel, not Leah, now holds. The order of the verse puts the child down to God's hearing, not to the plant or the bargain.

verses.context: A sixth son for Leah, Zebulun, and a last hope that her husband will honor her. Even with six sons Leah still speaks as one waiting for her husband's regard.
verses.grammar: Leah's speech has two wordplays. Zevadani Elohim oti zeved tov, ‘God has endowed me with a good endowment’, uses zavad, ‘to give a gift’, a rare word. Then yizbeleni ishi, ‘my husband will zabal me’, gives the name Zebulun. The meaning of zabal is uncertain. Many take it as ‘honor’ (the BSB's choice), connecting it with a Ugaritic word for a prince; others as ‘dwell with’, connecting it with zevul, a lofty dwelling (1 Kings 8:13 uses it of the temple). Either way Leah still hopes for Jacob's regard. Hapa'am ("This time") is the third time she has said it (29:34, 35).

verses.context: One short sentence records the birth of a daughter, Dinah. Unlike every son in this chapter, she receives no explanation of her name, but she is not forgotten: Genesis 34 tells her story, and her naming here prepares for it.
verses.grammar: The verse breaks the chain of narrative verb forms with ve'achar yaledah, ‘and afterward she bore’, a perfect after a time phrase that sets the birth slightly apart and signals a summary rather than the next step in a sequence. The name Dinah comes from the same root, din, as the name Dan in verse 6, ‘judgment’ or ‘justice’, a painful resonance given what happens to her in chapter 34.

theology.note: Genesis records Dinah's birth without comment and later lists her by name among Leah's children (46:15). The family history of Israel is told mostly through sons, and the verse is a reminder that the daughters were there too, though their stories are rarely told.

verses.context: The turning point of the chapter. After years of waiting, bargaining, and borrowed children, God remembers Rachel and she bears Joseph. Her words both look back (God has removed her disgrace) and look forward (may the LORD add another son).
verses.grammar: Three verbs make God the only actor: he remembered (vayyizkor), he listened (vayyishma), he opened (vayyiftach). The last repeats 29:31 exactly, where the LORD opened Leah's womb. Rachel's two speeches play on two different verbs: asaf Elohim et-cherpati, ‘God has gathered away my reproach’, uses asaf (‘gather, remove’), and yosef YHWH li ben acher, ‘may the LORD add to me another son’, uses yasaf (‘add’), which gives the name Joseph. Notice the change of divine name: the removal of disgrace is credited to Elohim, the general word for God, while the prayer for another son uses YHWH, the LORD, the covenant name.

theology.note: Rachel obtained the mandrakes, but she conceives only when God remembers her, and the verse credits nothing else. Human methods fill the middle of the chapter; this verse is where the narrator locates the real cause.

"He listened to her" assumes that Rachel had prayed, perhaps for years. Her new prayer for another son is answered in 35:17-18, at the cost of her life, a reminder that answered prayers in Scripture can carry sorrow as well as joy.

verses.context: Joseph's birth prompts Jacob to ask to go home. His request is framed as a worker's claim: he has served for his wives and children, and Laban knows how hard he worked. The second half of the chapter, a contest of shrewdness between two men, begins here.
verses.grammar: Shallecheni, "Send me on my way", is a Piel imperative of shalach, ‘send away, release’. It is the verb Moses will use to Pharaoh in "Let My people go" (Exodus 5:1), and several commentators note how Jacob's story in Haran anticipates Israel's in Egypt: hard service, a master who will not release the worker, wealth carried away, and a pursuit. The root avad (‘serve’) appears four times in verses 26 and 29 in noun and verb forms: Jacob measures his claim by his work.

verses.context: Laban, suddenly courteous, asks Jacob to stay and admits the reason: he has discovered that the LORD blesses him because of Jacob. He then offers to pay whatever Jacob names, the same open offer he made in 29:15 before the wedding trick.
verses.grammar: Im-na matsati chen be'enekha ("If I have found favor in your eyes") is the deferential formula of a petitioner, strange in the mouth of a master to his hired man. Nichashti, ‘I have learned by divination’, is discussed in the chapter note. Bigelalekha, ‘on account of you’, gives the reason for Laban's blessing: Jacob's presence. Nokvah sekharekha alay, "Name your wages", is literally ‘designate your wage upon me’, using naqav, ‘to specify’. The offer echoes Laban's question in 29:15 (though there the word for wages was maskoret), and a reader who remembers what followed that offer is on guard.

theology.note: God promised Abraham and then Jacob that all the families of the earth would be blessed through them (12:3, 28:14). Laban is the first foreigner in Jacob's story to experience that blessing, and he admits it, even though he learned it by a method Israel's law would forbid.

verses.context: Jacob answers by laying out his record: Laban had little before Jacob came, and the LORD has blessed him wherever Jacob went. Now Jacob wants to provide for his own household. His claim confirms Laban's admission and names the LORD as the source.
verses.grammar: Vayyifrots larov, ‘it has broken out into abundance’, uses parats, ‘to burst out, spread’, the verb of the Bethel promise (28:14) and of verse 43. Vayvarekh YHWH otkha leragli ("The LORD has blessed you wherever I set foot") is literally ‘the LORD has blessed you at my foot’, that is, following my steps. Matai e'eseh gam-anokhi leveti, ‘when will I also do for my own house’, uses the verb asah (‘do, make’) in the sense of providing, and the emphatic gam-anokhi, ‘I too’, sets Jacob's household beside Laban's.

verses.context: Jacob refuses a fixed wage and proposes a deal that looks modest: he will keep tending Laban's flocks and take as pay only the off-colored animals, which were few. He offers the arrangement as its own audit: any plain animal found in his flock can be counted as stolen.
verses.grammar: Lo-titten-li me'umah ("You do not need to give me anything") is emphatic: ‘you will give me nothing at all’. The pay categories are precise: naqod (‘speckled’), talu (‘spotted’, a passive participle, literally ‘patched’), and chum (‘dark’ or ‘brownish’) among the lambs. In verse 33 ve'anetah-bi tsidqati ("my honesty will testify for me") uses anah, ‘to answer’, in its legal sense of testifying, the verb of the commandment against false witness (Exodus 20:16). Tsedaqah, often ‘righteousness’, here means honest dealing in a contract. Ganuv ("stolen") prepares for chapter 31, where theft becomes the central charge between the two men.

verses.context: Laban agrees at once, then removes every animal that would qualify as Jacob's pay that same day and sends them off with his sons, three days' travel away. Jacob is left with only plain animals, from which his wages are supposed to come.
verses.grammar: Laban's reply, hen lu yehi khidvarekha, is effusive: ‘look, oh let it be as you say’. The particle lu expresses a wish, so the tone is eager agreement. Verse 35 then adds a new category, ‘streaked’ (aqqudim), and a telling phrase: kol asher-lavan bo, ‘every one that had white on it’. The word for white is lavan, the same letters as Laban's name, so the narrator's pun says that Laban removed everything with ‘Laban’ in it. Vayyitten beyad-banav, ‘he gave them into the hand of his sons’, is the first mention of Laban's sons, who will voice their resentment of Jacob in 31:1.

theology.note: Laban's agreement is a lie in all but words. He accepts the contract and in the same day empties it of value. The verse shows the pattern of 29:25 repeated: Laban keeps the letter of an agreement and breaks its purpose.

verses.context: Jacob responds with a breeder's trick. He peels fresh branches to show white stripes and sets them in the watering troughs where the animals mate, and the flocks bear streaked, speckled, and spotted young.
verses.grammar: The three trees are livneh (‘poplar’, a white tree whose name echoes lavan, ‘white’, and Laban), luz (‘almond’), and armon (‘plane tree’). Luz is also the old name of Bethel (28:19), the place where God promised to be with Jacob. Vayfatsel bahen petsalot levanot, ‘he peeled in them white peelings’, doubles the root patsal (‘peel’) and then names the exposed wood hallavan, ‘the white’. With the poplar, the white sound runs through the verse three times, as Jacob outwits the man whose name means white.

theology.note: The narrator reports the branches but credits the result elsewhere: Jacob will later tell his wives that God showed him in a dream which males were mating, and that God took Laban's livestock and gave it to him (31:9-12). Human method and divine provision sit side by side, and Scripture places the decisive cause with God.

verses.context: Jacob separates his own growing flock and arranges Laban's animals to face the streaked and dark ones. He then keeps his flocks apart, so the two herds grow as distinct property.
verses.grammar: This is one of the more obscure verses in Genesis. Hifrid Ya'aqov ("Jacob set apart") is clear, but the next clause, vayyitten pene hatstson el-aqod vekhol-chum betson Lavan, ‘he set the faces of the flock toward the streaked and every dark one in Laban's flock’, is ambiguous. It seems to mean that Jacob used his own off-colored animals, as he had used the branches, to stand in the breeding animals' line of sight. Vayyashet lo adarim levaddo, ‘he made for himself flocks by themselves’, uses shit, ‘to set, place’, and the negative clause that follows repeats the point.
verses.text: English translations differ noticeably here because the Hebrew is compressed. Some, like the BSB, have Jacob make "the rest face the streaked dark-colored sheep in Laban's flocks"; others read the flocks as facing the streaked and dark animals that were now Jacob's. The general sense, that Jacob separated and arranged the flocks to his advantage, is not in doubt.

verses.context: Jacob uses the branches only when the stronger animals are breeding. The result is that the weak animals go to Laban and the strong to Jacob, a strategy of selective breeding that works whatever one thinks of the branches.
verses.grammar: Hammequssharot, "the stronger females", is a Pual participle of qashar, ‘to bind’, so literally ‘the tightly knit ones’, meaning sturdy or robust. The opposite is ha'atufim, "the weaker", from atap, ‘to be feeble’. Both verses use consecutive perfects (vehayah, vesam) to describe what Jacob did repeatedly, breeding season after breeding season. The contrast of strong and feeble in verse 42 is the chapter's verdict on the contest: the plain ones went to Laban.

verses.context: The chapter ends with a summary of Jacob's wealth. The fugitive who crossed the Jordan with only a staff (32:10) is now rich in flocks, servants, camels, and donkeys, and the Bethel promise of increase has begun to be kept.
verses.grammar: Vayyifrots ha'ish me'od me'od, ‘the man broke out very, very much’, uses the doubled adverb me'od me'od, one of Hebrew's strongest ways of saying ‘exceedingly’. The same doubling appears in God's promise to multiply Abraham (17:2) and in the description of Israel's growth in Egypt (Exodus 1:7). The verb parats again recalls 28:14. The list of possessions closely matches what Abram acquired in Egypt (12:16), another hint that the patriarchs' stories foreshadow one another.
verses.history: Camels appear throughout the patriarchal stories, and their presence is a debated historical question. Some archaeologists argue that camels were not widely domesticated in the southern Levant until around the end of the second millennium BC and see the references as details from a later period; others point to earlier evidence for camels in Mesopotamia and Arabia and argue that a few wealthy households could have owned them. The debate concerns how the stories were told and transmitted, and the text's point is plain either way: Jacob became rich.

theology.note: The wealth is the covenant blessing in visible form, the first installment of the promise that Jacob would spread out in every direction (28:14). Jacob will later confess that this came from God's faithfulness, not his own cleverness (32:10).
